standard.title: Creative sentence variation for effect
standard.description: identify how authors vary sentence structures creatively for effects, such as intentionally using a dependent clause on its own or a sentence fragment
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how complex and compound-complex sentences elaborate, extend and explain ideas (AC9E7LA05). They have not yet examined how authors deliberately violate sentence conventions as a creative device.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify how authors use intentional structural violations — dependent clauses as sentences, sentence fragments, interrupting clauses — to achieve deliberate effects.

nodes.label: Identifying intentional structural violations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between unintentional sentence errors and deliberate structural violations used for effect.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one example of a deliberate structural violation (fragment or dependent clause used as a sentence) and explain why it is intentional rather than an error.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and distinguish intentional sentence fragments, stand-alone dependent clauses, and interrupting clauses in published texts, explaining the markers that signal deliberate rather than erroneous use.
wider: Compare how structural violations in literary fiction versus advertising create different effects — and different conventions about when violation is acceptable
Examine how spoken language conventions (incomplete sentences, interruptions) are imported into written texts for particular effects

response_modes.reason: The concept of intentional violation is confusing for students who have been taught that fragments are 'wrong'. Multiple contexts — literary, advertising, journalism — each have different tolerance for structural violation and different effects. Breadth across contexts resolves the apparent rule-violation confusion.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish intentional from erroneous violations cannot analyse effects at N2 and N3 — they have no principled basis for treating a fragment as a device rather than a mistake to ignore.
success_criteria: Student identifies a structural violation and names the type (fragment, stand-alone dependent clause, interrupting clause)
Student provides a reason for treating it as intentional (e.g. author, publication context, consistency of device, effect achieved)

nodes.label: Effect of sentence fragments and stand-alone clauses
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify how sentence fragments and stand-alone dependent clauses create specific effects — emphasis, rhythm, voice, immediacy.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a sentence fragment or stand-alone dependent clause and explain the specific effect it creates (e.g. emphasis, pause, urgency).
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how fragments, stand-alone dependent clauses and their placement in the surrounding prose create effects of emphasis, rhythm or voice in literary or persuasive texts.
wider: Compare the effect of a fragment at the start versus end of a paragraph, and analyse how position interacts with the device
Examine how fragments are used differently in first-person narrative versus third-person, and what this reveals about voice and reader positioning

response_modes.reason: Students who can identify fragments still often produce generic effect labels ('it creates tension'). Comparing fragment effects across different positions and genres — and examining what changes and what stays constant — builds the analytical precision needed to move beyond generic effect labelling.

success_criteria: Student identifies the structural violation and names a specific effect it creates
Student explains how the effect connects to the surrounding text — not just the fragment in isolation

nodes.label: Interrupting clauses and their effects
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify how interrupting clauses (embedded inside another clause) create effects of qualification, digression, intimacy or irony.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify an interrupting clause in a text and explain how its placement within another clause creates a specific effect on pace, voice or meaning.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how interrupting clauses are used across literary and informational texts to create qualification, digression, intimacy or irony, explaining the effect of the interruption on reader experience.
wider: Compare how the same type of interrupting clause (e.g. parenthetical aside) creates very different effects in fiction versus formal academic writing
Examine how writers use interrupting clauses to mimic the rhythms of thought or spoken language in stream-of-consciousness or first-person narrative

response_modes.reason: This node completes the set — fragments, stand-alone clauses, interrupting clauses — as a coordinated toolkit of intentional sentence variation. Students are building an integrated understanding of structural violation as a legitimate authorial resource, not three separate tricks.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Intentional sentence variation connects to authorial voice, style and genre conventions — rich territory for Y9 writers as well as readers. Advancing students can explore how these devices construct distinctive prose styles across authors, which supports both literary analysis and creative writing.
success_criteria: Student identifies an interrupting clause (naming the outer and inner clause structure)
Student explains a specific effect the interruption creates — not just that it 'adds detail'
